lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Symptoms, Effects and Prevention of Communicable Diseases

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Compile data on the number of males and females who suffer from common communicable diseases such as hepatitis, from a medical centre, and determine the possible causes of these diseases.
- Identify causes, symptoms, effects and prevention of hepatitis, HIV, measles and others, and make a presentation.
- Search for the causes, symptoms and prevention of hepatitis, and develop a plan to minimise the disease.

pages.title: What is a Communicable Disease?
pages.body: A communicable disease is an illness caused by a microorganism, such as a virus or bacterium, that can spread from one person to another, or from an animal to a person. Hepatitis, HIV and measles are three common communicable diseases studied at this level, each caused by a different virus, spread in different ways, and requiring different prevention measures.

questions.q: A communicable disease is best described as an illness that
o: Can spread from one person to another or from animals to people
Is caused only by poor diet
questions.e: A communicable disease is an illness caused by a microorganism, such as a virus or bacterium, that can spread from one person to another, or from an animal to a person.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Causes, Symptoms and Prevention of Common Communicable Diseases

pages.title: Causes, Symptoms and Prevention of Common Communicable Diseases
pages.body:
Cause, common symptoms and prevention are three key pieces of information needed to understand and respond appropriately to any communicable disease, as summarised in the table below.

| **DISEASE** | **CAUSE** | **COMMON SYMPTOMS** | **PREVENTION** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hepatitis** | A virus that infects and damages the liver, spread through infected blood, body fluids or contaminated food and water | Fatigue, yellowing of the skin and eyes, abdominal pain, nausea | Vaccination, safe food and water practices, avoiding contact with infected blood |
| **HIV** | A virus that attacks the body's immune system, spread mainly through infected blood and certain body fluids | May show no early symptoms, later fatigue, weight loss, frequent infections | Avoiding unprotected sexual contact, avoiding sharing needles, safe blood screening |
| **Measles** | A virus spread through coughing and sneezing, or contact with infected droplets in the air | Fever, cough, red eyes, a distinctive skin rash | Vaccination, isolating infected individuals, good hygiene |

pages.title: Effects of Communicable Diseases
pages.body: Health effects, economic effects, and social effects are three broad categories of impact that communicable diseases can have on individuals, families and communities. Health effects range from mild, short term illness to severe, long term complications or, in serious untreated cases, death. Economic effects include the cost of treatment, lost income during illness, and reduced productivity. Social effects can include stigma or discrimination against people living with certain diseases, which is why accurate, compassionate public education about how these diseases actually spread is so important.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Developing a Plan to Minimise Disease

pages.title: Developing a Plan to Minimise Disease
pages.body: Vaccination, safe practices, early detection, and public education are four key elements of an effective plan to minimise the spread of a communicable disease such as hepatitis in a community. Vaccination, where available, protects individuals before they are exposed to the disease. Safe practices, such as proper food handling, clean water, and safe medical procedures, reduce opportunities for the disease to spread. Early detection, through regular health checkups, allows treatment to begin before the disease worsens or spreads further. Public education helps community members understand how a disease spreads and how to protect themselves and others, while also reducing stigma against those affected.

pages.title: More About Hepatitis, HIV and Measles
pages.body:
| **DISEASE** | **HOW IT SPREADS** | **SIGNS AND EFFECTS** | **PREVENTION AND CONTROL** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hepatitis A and hepatitis E** | Through food and water contaminated with faeces | Tiredness, loss of appetite, nausea, dark urine, pale stools and jaundice, which is yellowing of the skin and eyes. The illness is usually short | Clean drinking water, proper toilets, washing hands with soap and washing fruits and vegetables |
| **Hepatitis B and hepatitis C** | Through infected blood and body fluids. This includes unprotected sex, sharing needles, razors and toothbrushes, unscreened blood and, for hepatitis B, from mother to baby at birth | May show no signs for years. The infection can last for life and lead to scarring of the liver and liver cancer | Hepatitis B vaccine, which babies in Ghana receive as part of routine immunisation. Screening of blood, and not sharing sharp objects. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C |
| **HIV** | Through unprotected sex, infected blood, sharing sharp objects, and from mother to child during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding. It is not spread by shaking hands, sharing food or mosquito bites | The virus slowly destroys the cells that defend the body. Without treatment this leads to AIDS, in which the body cannot fight infections | Abstinence, faithfulness to one partner, correct use of condoms, testing, and medicines for pregnant mothers who have the virus. There is no cure, but antiretroviral medicines control the virus so that a person can live a long life |
| **Measles** | Through droplets from coughs and sneezes. It spreads very easily | High fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes and a rash. It can lead to pneumonia, blindness, swelling of the brain and death, especially in young children who are poorly fed | Measles vaccine, which children in Ghana receive at 9 months and again at 18 months. Keep the sick child away from other children |

HIV stands for human immunodeficiency virus and AIDS stands for acquired immune deficiency syndrome. HIV is the virus and AIDS is the late stage of the infection. A person can carry HIV for many years and look healthy, which is why testing is important.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Ghana Health Service and the Ministry of Health run various national programmes, including immunisation campaigns for diseases such as measles and hepatitis, aimed at reducing the number of new cases across the country. Understanding these diseases at a basic level helps young people make informed decisions about their own health and supports community efforts to reduce the spread of communicable disease.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Search for information that is associated with communicable diseases.
- Create awareness about risk factors of communicable diseases such as hepatitis, HIV, measles and others, in order to prevent the diseases in schools and communities.

pages.title: What is a Risk Factor?
pages.body: A risk factor is any condition, behaviour or circumstance that increases the likelihood of a person getting or spreading a disease. Understanding risk factors helps individuals and communities identify where they are most vulnerable, so that they can take targeted action to reduce their chances of becoming infected or passing an infection on to others.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Common Risk Factors for Communicable Diseases

pages.title: Common Risk Factors for Communicable Diseases
pages.body:
Poor hygiene, unsafe water and food, overcrowding, limited healthcare access, low vaccination coverage, and unsafe practices are six common risk factors that increase the chances of communicable disease spreading in a community, as summarised in the table below.

| **RISK FACTOR** | **WHY IT INCREASES RISK** |
|---|---|
| **Poor personal hygiene** | Increases the chance of picking up and spreading infectious microorganisms |
| **Unsafe water and food practices** | Allows disease causing microorganisms to enter the body through contaminated water or food |
| **Overcrowded living conditions** | Makes it easier for diseases spread through the air or close contact to pass between people |
| **Limited access to healthcare** | Delays diagnosis and treatment, allowing a disease to progress further or spread to others |
| **Low vaccination coverage** | Leaves more people vulnerable to diseases that vaccines could otherwise prevent |
| **Unsafe medical or personal practices** | Such as sharing needles or unscreened blood, can directly transmit certain infections |

pages.title: Analysing Risk in a School or Community Setting
pages.body: Identifying specific risk factors, understanding why they matter, and targeting appropriate action are three steps involved in analysing the risk of communicable disease in a particular setting. A school with shared toilet facilities and limited hand washing stations, for example, faces an increased risk from poor hygiene, which could be addressed by installing more hand washing points and educating students on proper handwashing technique. A community relying on an unprotected well may face increased risk from unsafe water, which could be addressed by treating the water or protecting the well from contamination.

pages.title: Creating Awareness About Risk Factors
pages.body: Clear, accurate, non judgemental information about risk factors is essential for effective disease prevention, since awareness campaigns that shame or exclude people associated with certain risk factors can discourage them from seeking help or being honest about their health, ultimately making disease control harder rather than easier. Effective awareness campaigns focus on practical actions people can take, such as improving hygiene, safe water practices, and seeking vaccination, rather than blaming individuals for their circumstances.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Some risk factors, such as overcrowding or limited healthcare access, are linked to wider social and economic conditions that cannot be solved by individual behaviour alone. This is why effective disease prevention often requires action at multiple levels, from individual hygiene practices, to school and community programmes, to government policies that improve healthcare access and living conditions across the country.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Bacterial Diseases, Food Poisoning, Gonorrhoea and Meningitis

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Discuss the nature of bacterial diseases.
- Search for information and make presentations on food poisoning, gonorrhoea and meningitis diseases and their mode of transmission from person to person, community to community and from country to country.
- Describe the symptoms, effects and prevention of food poisoning, gonorrhoea and meningitis diseases.
- Describe the role of individuals, community members and government in managing food poisoning, gonorrhoea and meningitis diseases.
- Design and produce a poster to educate community members on the incidence and control of food poisoning, gonorrhoea and meningitis.

pages.title: The Nature of Bacterial Diseases
pages.body: A bacterial disease is an illness caused by harmful bacteria entering and multiplying within the body, disrupting normal body functions. Unlike viral diseases, many bacterial diseases can be treated effectively with antibiotics, provided they are diagnosed and treated early, before the bacteria multiply extensively or become resistant to treatment. Food poisoning, gonorrhoea and meningitis are three bacterial diseases studied at this level, each caused by different bacteria and spread in different ways.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Causes, Symptoms and Prevention of Selected Bacterial Diseases

pages.title: Causes, Symptoms and Prevention of Selected Bacterial Diseases
pages.body:
Mode of transmission, common symptoms and prevention measures are three key pieces of information for understanding food poisoning, gonorrhoea and meningitis, as summarised in the table below.

| **DISEASE** | **MODE OF TRANSMISSION** | **COMMON SYMPTOMS** | **PREVENTION** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Food poisoning** | Eating food or drinking water contaminated with harmful bacteria | Stomach pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever | Proper food handling, thorough cooking, clean water, good hygiene |
| **Gonorrhoea** | Sexual contact with an infected person | Pain during urination, unusual discharge, in some cases no early symptoms | Avoiding unprotected sexual contact, prompt treatment, open communication with partners |
| **Meningitis** | Close contact with an infected person through respiratory droplets | Severe headache, stiff neck, fever, sensitivity to light | Vaccination, avoiding overcrowded spaces during outbreaks, prompt medical attention |

pages.title: How These Diseases Spread, from Person to Person to Across Countries
pages.body: Person to person contact, community level spread, and international spread are three levels at which bacterial diseases can move, depending on how easily the responsible bacteria transmit and how much people travel and interact. Food poisoning can spread within a household if contaminated food is shared, and can affect an entire community if a shared water source or market food supply becomes contaminated. Gonorrhoea can spread through sexual contact between individuals and can appear in multiple communities as infected individuals travel or have contact with new partners. Meningitis can spread quickly in crowded settings, such as schools or dormitories, and has, in some outbreaks, spread across regions and even across national borders, particularly in areas prone to seasonal outbreaks.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Role of Individuals, Communities and Government

pages.title: The Role of Individuals, Communities and Government
pages.body: Personal responsibility, community cooperation, and government action are three levels of responsibility involved in managing bacterial diseases such as food poisoning, gonorrhoea and meningitis. Individuals can practise good hygiene, safe food handling, and responsible personal behaviour, and can seek prompt medical attention when symptoms appear. Communities can support clean water supplies, safe food markets, and awareness campaigns. Governments can provide healthcare services, run vaccination programmes where available, regulate food safety standards, and respond quickly to disease outbreaks with public health measures.

pages.title: The Bacteria Responsible and Further Facts
pages.body:
| **DISEASE** | **BACTERIA RESPONSIBLE** | **FURTHER FACTS** | **TREATMENT AND CONTROL** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Food poisoning** | Bacteria such as Salmonella and Staphylococcus | Signs appear within hours to a few days of eating contaminated food. The main danger is loss of water and salts from the body through vomiting and diarrhoea | Oral rehydration salts and plenty of fluids. See a health worker if it is severe. Wash hands, cook food well, cover food and keep it away from flies |
| **Gonorrhoea** | Neisseria gonorrhoeae | It is a sexually transmitted infection. Many infected females show no early signs. If it is not treated it can cause infertility in both males and females. A mother can pass it to the eyes of her baby during birth | Antibiotics from a health facility for both partners. Abstinence, faithfulness and correct use of condoms |
| **Meningitis** | Neisseria meningitidis causes cerebrospinal meningitis | It is an infection of the coverings of the brain and spinal cord. It is spread by droplets and is most common in the northern parts of Ghana in the dry season. It can kill within a day or two, and survivors may lose their hearing | Urgent treatment with antibiotics in hospital. Vaccination, good ventilation of rooms and avoiding overcrowding |

Antibiotics must be taken exactly as prescribed and the full course must be finished. Stopping early or using antibiotics without a prescription allows bacteria to become resistant, so that the medicines no longer work.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Ghana lies within a region of West Africa sometimes called the meningitis belt, where seasonal outbreaks of meningitis have historically been more common, particularly during the dry season. This is one reason meningitis vaccination campaigns and public health monitoring are especially important in parts of the country, and it shows how understanding a disease's mode of transmission and regional patterns can directly inform prevention strategies.
